title: Columnwise quasi-isomorphism comparison for uniformly bounded-above double complexes
statement: Let C be an abelian category [def-sp-abelian], and let K,L be integer-indexed commuting double cochain complexes [def-sp-double-complex-total]. Suppose their total complexes exist. Let x0,y0 be integers such that K and L vanish as column complexes in first indices greater than x0, and every column of either complex vanishes in second indices greater than y0. For a morphism phi:K→L whose column morphisms phi.f i are quasi-isomorphisms for every integer i, the induced total morphism Tot(phi) is a quasi-isomorphism.

source.place: Lemma 12.25.3, finite-diagonal convergence; the comparison proof is formalized in WeilConjectures.FromJoel.Algebra.Homology.BicomplexColumns, total.quasiIso_map_of_isStrictlyGE_of_isStrictlyLE

proof.text: First consider a finite interval of columns [x,x0]. Induct on its length. For the empty interval both truncated double complexes and their totals are zero, hence the total map is a quasi-isomorphism. On adjoining the next column, the stupid filtration gives a degreewise split short exact sequence from the preceding truncation to the larger one, with quotient the single-column complex. Totalization preserves this sequence: every degreewise splitting of double-complex objects induces a splitting on their diagonal coproducts. The total of a single column is its vertical complex shifted by minus its first index. The quotient map is therefore a shift of a column quasi-isomorphism. The homology long exact sequences and the five lemma imply that the middle total map is a quasi-isomorphism.

Fix the homology degree n and retain columns with first index at least x=n-y0-1. For any total degree m in {n-1,n,n+1}, a removed first index p<x would force the second index q=m-p>y0, so its summand vanishes. Thus the inclusion of this stupid truncation into the original total is an isomorphism in the three degrees controlling homology at n, hence a quasi-isomorphism at n. Apply this to K and L. Naturality identifies the square formed by the two inclusions and the total maps. The finite-column comparison from the first step makes the truncated total map a quasi-isomorphism; cancellation with the two inclusion maps gives that Tot(phi) is a quasi-isomorphism at n. As n is arbitrary, it is a quasi-isomorphism.

proof_origin.place: Existing complete Lean proof, transcribed above; corresponds to the finite-diagonal argument of Stacks Tag 0132.
